peloton.name: Peloton
peloton.key_insight: Peloton's breakthrough insight was that fitness equipment isn't a product — it's a medium. The $2,000+ bike is a behavioral commitment device that creates sunk cost pressure to justify ongoing $44/month subscriptions. But the real retention engine is parasocial: instructors like Robin Arzón and Cody Rigsby are designed to feel like personal coaches who know you, creating an emotional bond that gym equipment alone can never generate. The live leaderboard adds competitive urgency (you can see your real-time rank among thousands of simultaneous riders), while high-fives from strangers simulate the social energy of a group fitness class. Peloton's post-pandemic challenge — 39% stock decline in 2022 — revealed the fragility of hardware-dependent behavioral lock-in: when users' sunk cost threshold was crossed, they abandoned the ecosystem entirely. The lesson is that parasocial motivation is powerful but insufficient when the financial commitment feels disproportionate to the perceived value.
peloton.top_technique: Parasocial Instructor Relationships as Retention Engine

uber.name: Uber
uber.key_insight: Uber is a case study in dual-sided behavioral design: the company applies behavioral science to both riders (friction elimination, surge anchoring) and drivers (gamification, loss aversion goals). The ethical tension is asymmetric — riders benefit from reduced friction, but drivers are nudged to work longer hours in ways that may not serve their interests. Uber's behavioral design works precisely because it's invisible: users don't know they're being nudged, and drivers don't realize the earnings goal is an anchor, not a recommendation.
